title: Wine and the tavern
hookLine: Hafiz's wine, tavern and beloved are symbols, and his readers argue about how literal
tomorrow: a Victorian traveler put Hafiz into English. did she get him?

cards: Inés went back to work, and on the drive home she had an idea: a small evening of poems, a long night with friends, the way families in Iran read Hafiz on Yalda. Zoe puts a Hafiz couplet on the invitation.
Theo, who grew up in a strict church, squints at it. A man named for knowing the Quran by heart, writing about wine? The Quran tells believers to leave strong drink aside.
So why is Hafiz's Divan full of it?

teach.h: STAIN YOUR PRAYER RUG WITH WINE.
teach.b: Start where the Divan starts. In its first ghazal, Hafiz says: stain your prayer rug with wine, if the elder of the Magians tells you to, because the traveler knows the ways of the road. That's the puzzle in one line.
Here's how his readers solve it, and they solve it two ways.

teach.h: READING ONE: THE LOVE OF GOD.
teach.b: The Sufi reading: the wine is the love of God, strong enough to drown the self. The tavern is where pretense is dropped.
The elder of the Magians is the spiritual guide, and staining the prayer rug means following love past a piety that's only for show.
Notice the Quran itself holds wine both ways: forbidden in this life, and promised as rivers in paradise.

teach.h: READING TWO: A JAB AT HYPOCRITES.
teach.b: The other reading hears a real cup and a real tavern, and a satirist taking aim. Hafiz mocks the preachers who put on a show in the pulpit, then go home and do something else in private.
For these readers, his target is hypocrisy, and the wine is the jab.
People who love Hafiz have argued for both. The puzzle doesn't need one answer. Hafiz keeps the wine moving, so you can't pin it down, and you have to think.

how: Persian readers and commentators read Hafiz's wine, tavern and beloved in more than one way: as Sufi symbols of divine love and the spiritual guide, or as real images used to mock religious hypocrisy. Both readings are taught.

games.q: what does “wine and the tavern” mean?
o: the inns where Persian poets once performed
Hafiz's images, read as God's love or as a real cup
a list of drinks served at Persian weddings

games.q: the first ghazal's strange line: tap the pairs.
p: the guide, in the Sufi reading
what the couplet says to stain with wine
a show in the pulpit, something else at home

s: it tells believers to leave strong drink aside, and it pictures rivers of wine in paradise.
readers of Hafiz still argue about how literal his wine is
some hear the love of God; some hear a real cup and a jab at hypocrites.
Hafiz's wine poems mean he cared nothing for the Quran
he was named for knowing it by heart; the wine is read as love of God, or as satire of fake piety.

games.q: at dinner, a cousin reads a Hafiz couplet about wine. an uncle bristles: 'that's a drinking song.' the cousin says: 'no, it's about God.' what fits how Hafiz is read?
o: readers hear it both ways, and Hafiz leaves room for both.
it's only about God; the wine is never a real cup.
it's only a drinking song; the God reading is a modern idea.
games.why: Sufi readers hear the love of God; others hear a real cup and a jab at hypocrites. Hafiz keeps the wine moving.

practice: Write one image from your own life by hand: a kitchen table, a locked door, a cup. Under it, write two readings, what it plainly is and what it might stand for. Leave both standing, and look at them through the quiet.

wordCard.voice: Wine and the tavern: Hafiz's images, heard as God's love and the heart's freedom, or as a real cup and a jab at show-off piety.

orig.note: Persian: wine. In Hafiz, read as a real cup or as the love of God.

carryVoice: Carry this: two readings, both left standing, the way Hafiz leaves them. Three days into Hafiz.
